extracted.intended_audience: aspiring authors, literary-philosophical writers, and young publishers
extracted.subtask_short: advice for authors and philosophical writing
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and stylistic guidance for writers—especially those producing philosophical or periodical works—including how to coin terms, handle symbolism and truth, avoid pedantry, and manage publication/subscription pitfalls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of symbols for highest ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: "An idea, in the highest sense of that word, cannot be conveyed but by a symbol; and, except in geometry, all symbols of necessity involve an apparent contradiction."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highest or most abstract ideas require symbolic expression; such symbols will often seem contradictory or opaque to casual readers ('the symbolic husk'), and the author should accept that his writings may not be intended for those who cannot 'pierce through' that symbolic form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Veracity is intention rather than literal utterance
rubrics_metrics.description: "Veracity does not consist in saying, but in the intention of communicating, truth; and the philosopher who cannot utter the whole truth without conveying falsehood... is constrained to express himself either mythically or equivocally."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When full disclosure would mislead, endanger, or provoke harmful passions, truthful intent can justify mythic or equivocal expression; moral truthfulness is judged by intention, not necessarily by literal explicitness.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to withhold explicit clarification
rubrics_metrics.description: The author may decline to settle disputed interpretations (example: Kant declining commentary) to avoid 'the honours of martyrdom' and because full clarification may be harmful or impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors may reasonably refuse to restate or fully explicate their meaning, especially if such exposition would be unsafe, futile, or self-defeating; a concise reply ('I meant what I said') can be defensible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware overbuilding systems with arbitrary notions (critique of Fichte)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fichte 'overbuilt with a heavy mass of mere notions, and psychological acts of arbitrary reflection,' leading to degeneration into 'crude egoismus' and ascetic ethics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing philosophical systems, avoid piling on gratuitous abstract notions or introspective artifices that disconnect the system from nature, human sympathies, or plausible ethics; favor coherence and avoid excessive speculative ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coin neologisms only to convey genuinely new senses
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: 'Esemplastic. The word is not in Johnson... I constructed it myself... to shape into one; because, having to convey a new sense, I thought that a new term would both aid the recollection of my meaning, and prevent its being confounded with the usual import of the word, imagination.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce new terms when existing words cannot convey a new or precise sense; a well-chosen neologism aids recollection and prevents confusion with established meanings, and is not necessarily pedantry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of pedantry: unsuitable language for time/place/company
rubrics_metrics.description: "If I am not misinformed, pedantry consists in the use of words unsuitable to the time, place, and company."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using technical or stylistically inappropriate language in contexts where it alienates or confuses the audience; pedantry can be committed by both the scholar (overlearned speech at a wine-table) and the man of the world (insisting on only colloquial terms in a scientific discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer new terms to old words with new meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: Using old words with new meanings 'demands a twofold exertion of thought' because the reader must learn the new definition and unlearn the habitual meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When precision requires altering an established word's meaning, prefer coining a new term to avoid forcing readers to suppress old associations; coinage reduces cognitive load compared to redefinition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restore obsolete terms when appropriately reclaimable
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an unappropriate term had 'without sufficient reason become obsolete, it is doubtless a less evil to restore than to coin anew.' Example: adopting 'sensuous' to cover perception as passive/recipient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an older term can be reclaimed to express a needed nuance (and not already fatally compromised), restoring it is acceptable and sometimes preferable to inventing entirely new vocabulary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate reuse of technical vocabulary with clear definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: re-introducing 'objective' and 'subjective', using 'intuition' both subjectively and objectively, and distinguishing 'reason' and 'understanding.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When recurring technical distinctions are essential, explicitly reintroduce or define established terms so they can be used conveniently and without confusion; consistency and careful discrimination of meanings is vital for metaphysical or theological speculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: First lesson of philosophic discipline: attend to kinds, not degrees
rubrics_metrics.description: "The first lesson of philosophic discipline is to wean the student's attention from the degrees of things... and to direct it to the kind abstracted from degree."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach and write so readers focus on abstract kinds and essential distinctions rather than merely comparative degrees; this enables clearer conceptual work in metaphysics, ethics, and theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid assuming audience competence; modulate technicality
rubrics_metrics.description: Pedant may 'over-rate the acquirements of his auditors' and thus converse at a wine-table with his mind fixed on his museum; conversely the man of the world who insists on only colloquial terms is also pedantic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match vocabulary and exposition to the audience's background: neither condescend to the lowest common denominator nor presume excessive technical familiarity; choose register appropriate to time/place/company.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not trust subscription lists uncritically
rubrics_metrics.description: Subscribers' names may be added without authority, extorted by zealous friends, or soon lapse (many 'threw up the publication before the fourth number'), so subscription counts are unreliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When planning periodical or subscription-based publishing, treat subscription tallies as provisional; anticipate drop-off, nonpayment, and that many names were added insincerely or under pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer selling copyright; avoid author+publisher combination
rubrics_metrics.description: "The most prudent mode is to sell the copy-right... By few only can a large remuneration be expected; but fifty pounds and ease of mind are of more real advantage... than the chance of five hundred with the certainty of insult and degrading anxieties."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unless you have the trade infrastructure and appetite for commercial risk, sell at least some editions' copyright to a bookseller: a modest guaranteed sum and reduced stress often outweigh speculative higher profits and the burdens of self-publishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not attempt to unite author and publisher's functions
rubrics_metrics.description: The author who 'attempts in any way to unite the functions of author and publisher' faces added expense, administrative burden, distribution problems, and social insults; trade practices may appear harsh but are entrenched.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the specialized role of booksellers/publishers; unless you can absorb extra costs, postal delays, and trade practices, rely on the ordinary trade to publish and distribute your work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of financial and logistical pitfalls of self-publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-publishing may require buying stamped paper, paying printing costs in advance, bearing postage and carriage, and losing substantial sums if subscribers fail to pay; examples include having to lay in a stock of stamped paper and paying extra percentages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Budget conservatively for upfront costs and delays; anticipate cashflow issues, postal slowness, editor/printer deadlines, and that revenue may lag publication by many weeks or months.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format, frequency, and price must suit audience habits
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: proposing a periodical of 'every eighth day, thirty-two pages, large octavo, price only four-pence' met audience resistance because many readers would not read that volume regularly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design format, length, frequency, and price to realistic reading habits and expectations; overly ambitious size/frequency can deter subscribers who cannot commit time or funds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect political or topical content to affect readership
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing an essay (e.g., 'against fast days') or shifting political stance cost the author hundreds of subscribers at once; changing tone alienates particular factions (Jacobins, democrats, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that political positions and topical attacks may rapidly shrink or shift your audience; plan content strategy with awareness of the likely partisan reactions and subscriber volatility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not vilify tradespeople for entrenched trade customs
rubrics_metrics.description: The author cautions against speaking 'unkindly or opprobriously' of booksellers, noting 'the individuals did not make the laws and customs of their trade.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique systemic trade practices if needed, but avoid personal animus toward individual booksellers; recognize systemic constraints rather than blaming practitioners for industry norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical humility: seek friendly, prudent counsel and allies
rubrics_metrics.description: The author recounts being rescued from financial ruin by a faithful friend who paid debts and gave wise advice; also notes the value of modest reception and helpful acquaintances during canvassing tours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate trustworthy friends, advisers, and local allies when undertaking publishing ventures; practical assistance and prudent counsel can avert ruin and offer moral support during failures.
